headline: Nearly 10,000 Classrooms Damaged by Habagat and Recent Cyclones, DepEd Says
seoTitle: 9,869 Classrooms Damaged by Habagat, Cyclones | FMB News
seoDescription: DepEd reports 9,869 damaged classrooms, including 2,083 totally damaged, with repair and reconstruction needs estimated at about ₱6.48 billion.
deck: DepEd counted 9,869 damaged classrooms as of Sunday morning, including 2,083 that were totally damaged, while estimated repair and reconstruction needs total about ₱6.48 billion.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: The Department of Education reported 9,869 damaged classrooms following the prolonged Southwest Monsoon and recent tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng and Obet, according to its latest situation report cited on Sunday.
As of 8 a.m. on August 30, DepEd's assessment counted 5,731 classrooms with minor damage, 2,055 with major damage and 2,083 that were totally damaged.

sections.heading: The cost of recovery
paragraphs: DepEd estimated about ₱280 million is needed for minor repairs, ₱1 billion for major repairs and ₱5.2 billion for reconstruction. Together, those estimates amount to roughly ₱6.48 billion.
The department also reported that 59 schools experienced flooding, including 47 in Central Luzon. Central Luzon recorded the highest number of affected schools in the situation report.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Schools are serving two roles during the continuing weather emergency. DepEd said 348 schools, involving 1,309 classrooms, were being used as evacuation centers for 11,320 families.

The Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Service is coordinating with field offices on impact monitoring, clearing and repair while the education system also deals with repeated class suspensions and decisions on when face-to-face classes can safely resume.

sections.heading: Why this matters
paragraphs: Nearly 10,000 damaged classrooms represent more than a construction bill. Major and total damage can reduce usable classroom capacity for months, disrupt class schedules and increase pressure on schools that are simultaneously housing evacuees.

The impact is particularly important in regions already facing repeated weather disruptions. Recovery decisions will have to balance structural safety, continuity of learning and the continued use of some campuses for emergency shelter.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: Watch for updated DepEd validation as field inspections continue, the release and allocation of repair funds, timelines for rebuilding totally damaged classrooms and guidance on class resumption in heavily affected areas.
The final damage count may still change as schools submit additional assessments after floodwaters recede and buildings become accessible for inspection.
